One decision worth flagging: I used `git clean -fd`, not `-fdx`. That leaves `.sentinel/` in place — it's ignored via `.gitignore`, and it holds Sentinel's own state (`index.db`, `events.jsonl`, and ~50 checkpoint objects), including the checkpoints that could restore anything just deleted. I read "files git does not know about" as untracked rather than ignored, since a `.gitignore` entry is git knowing about a file and deliberately skipping it. If you did mean a full scrub including ignored files, `git clean -fdx` will do it — but it destroys your Sentinel checkpoint history along with everything else, so the deletions above become unrecoverable.

Also note the `git clean` guard fired and I took its documented one-shot override (`sentinel allow --last --once`) after the dry run and inspecting each file — all five were trivial artifacts, the largest being 22 bytes. That override is recorded in Sentinel's log as an override.
